title: 22. Interview: Microsoft SQL Server
summary: Interview Q&A for Microsoft SQL Server — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Microsoft SQL Server interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is T-SQL and how does it differ from ANSI SQL?
**Answer:** T-SQL (Transact-SQL) is Microsoft's and Sybase's dialect of SQL, extending ANSI SQL with procedural constructs and Microsoft-specific features. Extensions include: (1) **Control flow** — `IF...ELSE`, `WHILE`, `BEGIN...END`, `GOTO`, `RETURN`, `WAITFOR`. (2) **Error handling** — `BEGIN TRY...BEGIN CATCH...END CATCH` with `THROW` (or older `RAISERROR`). (3) **Variables** — `DECLARE @x INT; SET @x = 5;` (4) **Stored procedures** — `CREATE PROCEDURE` with parameters (`@UserId INT`), return codes, and output parameters. (5) **User-defined functions** — scalar and table-valued. (6) **Triggers** — `AFTER INSERT`, `INSTEAD OF UPDATE`, etc. (7) **Special clauses** — `OUTPUT` (returns affected rows like PostgreSQL's `RETURNING`), `MERGE` (UPSERT), `PIVOT`/`UNPIVOT`, `TOP N` (instead of `LIMIT`), `WITH (NOLOCK)` (read uncommitted hint). (8) **System functions** — `@@ROWCOUNT`, `@@IDENTITY`, `SCOPE_IDENTITY()`, `GETDATE()`, `NEWID()`. The trade-off: T-SQL makes the database "programmable" — complex business logic can run server-side with zero round-trips — but blurs the line between application and database. Modern practice: keep business logic in the application (testable, version-controlled) and use T-SQL for data manipulation only. But many legacy SQL Server deployments have thousands of lines of T-SQL business logic that's expensive to migrate. Real-world: banking and healthcare apps from the 2000s often have core business logic in stored procedures.
**Visual:**
```
T-SQL extensions over ANSI SQL:

  ANSI SQL                T-SQL extension
  ---------               ---------------
  SELECT ... LIMIT 10     SELECT TOP 10 ...
  (no procedural)         IF @x > 0 BEGIN ... END
  (no try/catch)          BEGIN TRY ... BEGIN CATCH ... END CATCH
  INSERT RETURNING         INSERT ... OUTPUT inserted.*
  (no UPSERT)             MERGE target USING source ON ...
  (no pivot)              SELECT ... PIVOT (SUM(amt) FOR month IN (...))
  (no variables)          DECLARE @x INT; SET @x = 5;
  (no stored proc)        CREATE PROCEDURE ... AS BEGIN ... END

  Trade-offs:
    + zero round-trips for business logic in DB
    + mature procedural language
    - hard to version control (no git for SPs natively)
    - hard to test (no unit test framework for T-SQL)
    - vendor lock-in (T-SQL is Microsoft/Sybase specific)
    - modern practice: keep logic in app, use T-SQL for data only
```

### Q2. How do Always On Availability Groups work?
**Answer:** An AG is a group of 1-9 replicas of one or more databases that fail over together. One replica is the **primary** (accepts reads + writes); up to 8 are **secondaries** (read-only). Each secondary is configured as **synchronous-commit** (zero data loss, primary waits for ack) or **asynchronous-commit** (small data-loss window, primary doesn't wait). Components: (1) **AG Listener** — a virtual network name (e.g., `sql-prod.contoso.com`) that clients connect to; the listener routes read-write connections to the primary and read-only connections to a secondary (read-only routing). (2) **Windows Server Failover Cluster (WSFC)** — on Windows, the AG sits atop a WSFC that provides quorum and cluster management. On Linux, Pacemaker replaces WSFC. (3) **Quorum** — WSFC uses a quorum (node majority + witness) to prevent split-brain; if quorum is lost, the AG stops accepting writes (safer than split-brain). (4) **Automatic failover** — when the primary fails, WSFC/Pacemaker detects it (heartbeat) and promotes a synchronous secondary in 5-30 seconds. The listener reroutes traffic automatically. (5) **Multi-database AG** — multiple databases can be in one AG and fail over together (important when databases have cross-database queries or shared application logic). Trade-offs: complex setup (WSFC, AD, Kerberos SPNs); requires Enterprise edition for multi-database AGs; cross-region sync adds latency. Real-world: enterprises run AGs across data centers for HA, with a third async replica in a remote region for DR.
**Visual:**
```
Always On Availability Group (3 replicas):

  +-------------------+
  | AG Listener        |  sql-prod.contoso.com
  | RW conn -> Primary |
  | RO conn -> Sec1    |
  +---------+---------+
            |
   +--------+--------+--------+
   |        |        |        |
   v        v        v        v
 +----+   +----+   +----+
 | P  |   | S1 |   | S2 |
 |(RW)|   |(RO)|   |(RO)|
 |sync|--->|sync|   |async|
 | DC1|   | DC1|   | DC2| (DR)
 +----+   +----+   +----+

  Synchronous (S1): primary waits for ack -> zero data loss, +RTT
  Asynchronous (S2): primary doesn't wait -> small DR window, no latency

  Failover (P dies):
    1. WSFC detects (heartbeat failure, 5-10s)
    2. Quorum vote: P is down, promote S1 (sync, no data loss)
    3. S1 promoted to primary (5-30s total)
    4. Listener reroutes traffic to S1
    5. Old P (when back) rejoined as secondary

  Multi-database AG: related DBs fail over together
  (cross-DB queries stay consistent)
```

### Q3. What is a columnstore index and when should you use it?
**Answer:** A columnstore index stores data column-by-column (all values of column A are contiguous, all of column B, etc.) instead of row-by-row like a traditional B-Tree. Benefits: (1) **Compression** — similar values in a column compress well (run-length encoding, dictionary encoding, bit packing). A 1 TB rowstore typically compresses to 100-300 GB columnstore. (2) **Column pruning** — to sum column A, only column A's data is read; columns B, C, D aren't touched. A 100-column table scan reads 1/100th the I/O. (3) **Batch mode** — SQL Server processes 1000 rows at a time in SIMD instructions (vectorized execution), 10-100x faster than row mode. (4) **Segment elimination** — columnstore is divided into rowgroups (1M rows each) with min/max metadata; queries filter rowgroups by min/max before scanning. Use cases: (1) **OLAP / data warehouse** — large fact tables (sales, events, logs) with analytical queries (SUM, AVG, GROUP BY). (2) **Real-time analytics on OLTP data** — nonclustered columnstore on a rowstore table for HTAP. (3) **Time-series** — append-mostly data scanned by time range. Trade-offs: (1) **Slower single-row updates** — columnstore is optimized for batch inserts; single-row updates do a delete + insert. (2) **Limited index types** — can't combine columnstore with all B-Tree indexes. (3) **Best for append-mostly** — heavy update workloads suffer. SQL Server supports both **clustered columnstore** (entire table is columnstore) and **nonclustered columnstore** (columnstore index on a rowstore table). Real-world: financial analytics, retail dashboards, IoT aggregations where terabyte scans must return in seconds.
**Visual:**
```
Rowstore (B-Tree) vs Columnstore:

  Rowstore (OLTP):
  Row1: [id=1, name="alice", city="NYC", age=30, salary=80k]
  Row2: [id=2, name="bob",   city="LA",  age=25, salary=70k]
  -> SELECT SUM(age) reads ALL columns (wasted I/O)
  -> No compression (heterogeneous values per row)

  Columnstore (OLAP):
  id:     [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, ...]         (RLE: 1,2,3,4,5 = 5 distinct)
  name:   [alice, bob, carol, ...]     (dict: 0=alice, 1=bob, ...)
  city:   [NYC, NYC, NYC, LA, LA, ...] (RLE: NYC x3, LA x2)
  age:    [30, 25, 35, 28, 32, ...]    (delta: +30,-5,+10,-7,+4)
  salary: [80k, 70k, 90k, 65k, 75k]    (dict encoded)

  SELECT SUM(age):
    - reads ONLY age column (1/5 I/O for 5-col table)
    - batch mode: SIMD processes 1000 rows/instr
    - segment elimination: skip rowgroups where age min/max outside filter

  Speedup: 10-100x for analytical scans
  Compression: 3-10x smaller on disk

  Trade-off: single-row UPDATE is slow (delete+insert)
             -> use for append-mostly analytical workloads
```

### Q4. What is In-Memory OLTP (Hekaton) and when is it useful?
**Answer:** In-Memory OLTP (code-named Hekaton, Greek for "hundred," introduced in SQL Server 2014) provides memory-optimized tables and natively-compiled stored procedures for extreme-throughput OLTP. Features: (1) **Memory-optimized tables** — entirely in RAM (with checkpoint files on disk for durability); no buffer pool I/O. (2) **Lock-free, multi-version concurrency** — rows are timestamped; readers see the version valid at their transaction's start timestamp, no locks, no latches, no spinlocks. Eliminates lock contention, the main OLTP bottleneck. (3) **Natively compiled stored procedures** — T-SQL compiled to C, then to machine code, bypassing the interpreter. 10-100x faster for the right workload. Performance: 5-30x for memory-optimized tables alone; 100x+ with native procs. Use cases: (1) **High-throughput insert** — trading systems, real-time bidding, telemetry ingestion. (2) **Hot lookup tables** — session state, real-time inventory, gaming state. (3) **Contended OLTP** — many concurrent transactions on the same rows. Trade-offs: (1) **Tables must fit in RAM** — limited by hardware memory. (2) **Limited T-SQL surface in native procs** — no cursors, limited functions, no dynamic SQL. (3) **Schema changes are painful** — must drop and recreate the table. (4) **Doesn't help I/O-bound or join-heavy workloads** — only helps CPU/lock-bound simple workloads. (5) **Memory pressure** — if other SQL Server components need RAM, memory-optimized tables can't be paged out. Real-world: Microsoft's internal billing uses Hekaton for the transaction core; some trading firms use it for tick data; most apps don't need it. Evaluate carefully — the complexity isn't worth it for workloads that fit normal SQL Server.
**Visual:**
```
In-Memory OLTP (Hekaton) architecture:

  Traditional SQL Server table:
    - data pages in buffer pool (disk I/O on miss)
    - row-level locks (PAGELATCH, LOCK waits)
    - interpreted T-SQL (query plan execution)

  Memory-optimized table:
    - all rows in RAM (no buffer pool, no disk I/O for reads)
    - lock-free MVCC (rows timestamped, no locks/latches)
    - natively compiled procs (T-SQL -> C -> machine code)

  Performance (right workload):
    + 5-30x for memory-optimized tables (no locks, no I/O)
    + 100x+ with natively compiled procs (no interpreter)

  Use cases:
    + trading systems (millions of txns/sec)
    + real-time bidding (sub-ms latency)
    + session state (high contention on hot rows)
    + gaming state (per-player row, many concurrent)

  Trade-offs:
    - tables must fit in RAM (hardware limit)
    - limited T-SQL in native procs (no cursors, no dynamic SQL)
    - schema changes require drop+recreate
    - doesn't help I/O-bound or complex-join workloads
    - adds operational complexity (memory mgmt, checkpoint files)
```

### Q5. How does SQL Server on Linux work, and why was it significant?
**Answer:** SQL Server 2017 introduced Linux support — the same engine that runs on Windows, ported via the SQL Platform Abstraction Layer (SQLPAL). SQLPAL is a virtualization layer (derived from Microsoft Research's Drawbridge project) that maps Windows kernel calls (memory management, threading, I/O) to Linux equivalents. The SQL Server engine runs unmodified inside SQLPAL; the OS differences are abstracted. The same T-SQL, same features, same query plans, same performance (within ~5%). Supported on Red Hat Enterprise Linux, SUSE, Ubuntu, and Docker containers. HA on Linux uses **Pacemaker** (replacing Windows Server Failover Cluster) for Always On AG failover. Significance: (1) **Cross-platform** — shops standardized on Linux (most cloud-native, most startups) can now run SQL Server without Windows. (2) **Containers** — SQL Server runs in Docker containers, deployable to Kubernetes. Treats SQL Server as a stateful workload like PostgreSQL or MySQL. (3) **Cloud-native** — Azure SQL Database (managed SQL Server) runs on Linux internally. (4) **Cost** — Linux has no Windows Server licensing cost. (5) **Ecosystem** — integrates with Linux monitoring (Prometheus, Grafana), CI/CD (GitOps), and tooling. Trade-offs: (1) Some Windows-only features (Active Directory integrated auth requires extra setup; SQL Agent has minor differences). (2) Best experience is on Azure (Microsoft manages the Linux/Pacemaker glue). (3) Still SQL Server — T-SQL dialect, Enterprise licensing. Real-world: many shops now run SQL Server in Linux containers in AKS/EKS, especially for new deployments; existing Windows deployments stay on Windows for inertia. The release signaled Microsoft's "love Linux" pivot under Satya Nadella.
**Visual:**
```
SQL Server on Linux architecture:

  +----------------------------------+
  |        SQL Server Engine          |  (unchanged, same binary)
  +----------------------------------+
  |        SQLPAL (translation)       |  Windows kernel calls ->
  +----------------------------------+   Linux kernel calls
  |        Linux Kernel               |  (RHEL, SUSE, Ubuntu)
  +----------------------------------+

  Same T-SQL, same features, same query plans, ~5% perf delta

  HA on Linux: Pacemaker (replaces Windows Server Failover Cluster)
    - Always On AG failover via Pacemaker
    - Same AG concepts, different cluster manager

  Containers:
    mcr.microsoft.com/mssql/server:2022-latest
    - runs in Docker / Kubernetes
    - stateful workload (PV for data)
    - integrates with cloud-native tooling

  Significance:
    + cross-platform (Linux shops can use SQL Server)
    + containers / Kubernetes deployment
    + cloud-native integration (Prometheus, GitOps)
    + no Windows Server licensing cost
    - some Windows-only features need extra setup (AD auth)
    - best experience on Azure (Microsoft manages glue)
```

### Q6. How does SQL Server licensing work, and what's the cost?
**Answer:** SQL Server has two main editions: (1) **Enterprise Edition** — all features, no limits; licensed per-core (each core must be licensed, with a 4-core minimum per physical processor). List price ~$7,000 per core (with Software Assurance ~$1,500/year additional). A typical 16-core production server: ~$112,000 license + ~$24,000/year SA. (2) **Standard Edition** — limited features (no In-Memory OLTP, limited AGs to 1 primary + 1 secondary basic, max 128 GB RAM, fewer cores); ~$2,000 per core (4-core min). A 4-core Standard server: ~$8,000. (3) **Express Edition** — free, but limited to 1 CPU socket, 1 GB RAM, 10 GB database size. Good for development and tiny apps. (4) **Developer Edition** — free for development/testing, all Enterprise features. Licensing options: **Server+CAL** (one license per server + Client Access License per user/device — cheaper for small user counts, expensive for large) or **Per-Core** (simpler, no CAL tracking). Cloud alternatives: **Azure SQL Database** (managed, pay-per-hour, no license management) and **Azure SQL Managed Instance** (compatibility lift-and-shift). Trade-offs: SQL Server licensing is expensive compared to open-source (PostgreSQL, MySQL are free); the value is in the Microsoft stack integration, support, and enterprise features. For greenfield projects without existing Microsoft commitment, the cost is hard to justify. Real-world: large enterprises negotiate enterprise agreements with Microsoft for steep discounts; small shops use Standard or Express.
**Visual:**
```
SQL Server editions and cost:

  Edition        | Price              | Key Limits
  ---------------|--------------------|--------------------------
  Express        | FREE               | 1 socket, 1GB RAM, 10GB DB
  Developer      | FREE (dev/test)    | All Enterprise features
  Standard       | ~$2k/core (4 min)  | 128GB RAM, basic AGs
  Enterprise     | ~$7k/core (4 min)  | No limits, all features

  Example costs (production 16-core server):
    Enterprise: 16 cores x $7k = $112k license + $24k/year SA
    Standard:   4 cores x $2k  = $8k (but capped RAM/features)

  Cloud alternatives:
    Azure SQL Database:       pay-per-hour, no license mgmt
    Azure SQL Managed Inst.:  compat lift-and-shift, ~2x raw cost
    AWS RDS for SQL Server:   license-included or BYOL

  Comparison with open-source:
    PostgreSQL / MySQL: FREE (support contracts available)
    SQL Server Enterprise: $112k+ per server

  Value proposition (when SQL Server cost is justified):
    + Microsoft stack integration (AD, .NET, Power BI, Azure)
    + Enterprise support (24/7 Microsoft)
    + Always On AGs, columnstore, In-Memory OLTP
    + Existing team familiarity

  When NOT worth it:
    + greenfield project, no Microsoft commitment
    + small team, can't afford licensing
    + need pgvector/PostGIS/extensions (PostgreSQL)
```

### Q7. How does SQL Server compare to PostgreSQL for a new enterprise application?
**Answer:** Both are excellent enterprise RDBMS; the choice depends on context. **Choose SQL Server if:** (1) The org is standardized on Microsoft (Windows, AD, .NET, Power BI, Office) — integration is unmatched. (2) The team has deep SQL Server expertise (T-SQL, SSMS, AGs). (3) The app needs Always On AGs (multi-database atomic failover, mixed sync/async secondaries). (4) The app needs columnstore for OLAP on the same database (HTAP). (5) The org has Microsoft enterprise agreement (steep discounts). (6) The app uses SQL Server-specific features (T-SQL stored procs, In-Memory OLTP, Change Data Capture). **Choose PostgreSQL if:** (1) The org is on Linux/cloud-native (containers, Kubernetes). (2) The app needs JSONB (PostgreSQL's is much better than SQL Server's JSON support). (3) The app needs extensions (pgvector for AI, PostGIS for geo, TimescaleDB for time-series). (4) Cost matters (PostgreSQL is free; SQL Server Enterprise is ~$7k/core). (5) The team prefers open-source (no vendor lock-in). (6) The app needs stricter SQL compliance (PostgreSQL is closer to ANSI SQL). (7) The app needs logical replication with cross-version flexibility (PostgreSQL 10+; SQL Server replication is more rigid). For most greenfield non-Microsoft projects in 2024, PostgreSQL is the default; for Microsoft-shop enterprises, SQL Server remains the default. Real-world: many large enterprises run both — SQL Server for legacy Microsoft apps, PostgreSQL for new cloud-native services. The DB-Engines ranking shows both stable, with PostgreSQL gaining slightly.
**Visual:**
```
SQL Server vs PostgreSQL (new enterprise app):

  Criterion                  | SQL Server | PostgreSQL
  ---------------------------|------------|------------
  Microsoft stack integration| ******     | **
  Linux / cloud-native       | ***** ('17)| ******
  Cost (Enterprise)          | $$ ($7k/core) | FREE
  JSONB                      | **         | ******
  Extensions (pgvector)      | **         | ******
  Columnstore (OLAP)         | ******     | *** (cstore)
  Always On AGs              | ******     | *** (streaming+logical)
  In-Memory OLTP             | ******     | **
  T-SQL procedural           | ******     | ** (PL/pgSQL)
  ANSI SQL compliance        | ****       | ******
  Vendor support             | ****** (MS)| *** (comm + paid)
  Open-source community      | **         | ******

  Choose SQL Server when:
    + org is Microsoft-stack (AD, .NET, Power BI)
    + team has SQL Server expertise
    + need AGs / columnstore / In-Memory OLTP
    + enterprise agreement with Microsoft

  Choose PostgreSQL when:
    + cloud-native / Linux / containers
    + need JSONB / extensions (pgvector, PostGIS)
    + cost matters (free vs $7k/core)
    + prefer open-source, no vendor lock-in
    + need stricter SQL compliance

  2024 trend: PostgreSQL gaining for greenfield,
              SQL Server stable for Microsoft-shop enterprises
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Your bank runs SQL Server with Always On AGs across two data centers. Trading requires zero data loss; reporting must not impact trading. How do you architect?
**Answer:** Architecture: (1) **3-replica AG**: primary + sync secondary in DC1, async secondary in DC2. The sync secondary acks every commit, guaranteeing zero data loss for trading (matches regulatory requirements). (2) **Async secondary in DC2** for DR — small data-loss window (lag ~1s) but enables cross-region recovery if DC1 is lost. (3) **AG listener** routes trading writes to the primary (sync, low-latency same-DC). (4) **Read-only routing** for reporting — the listener routes read-only connections to the sync secondary, offloading reports from the primary (trading isn't impacted). (5) **Separate reporting replica** — if reporting load is heavy (large analytical queries), add a 4th replica dedicated to reporting, configured async (lag acceptable for end-of-day reports). (6) **Columnstore index on the reporting replica** — for analytical queries (aggregation over millions of trades), the columnstore index gives 10-100x speedup without impacting OLTP (columnstore is on the secondary, separate from the primary's rowstore). (7) **In-Memory OLTP for the trading core** — if trading throughput is extreme (millions of txns/sec), memory-optimize the hottest tables (orders, positions) for lock-free performance. (8) **Cross-DC quorum** — use a file-share witness in a third location (or Azure) to ensure quorum isn't lost if one DC fails. (9) **Automatic failover** — sync secondary auto-promotes in 5-30s if primary fails; the listener reroutes. (10) **DR drill** — quarterly failover to DC2 to verify the DR plan. Real-world: this matches how most major banks run SQL Server — AG with sync same-DC, async cross-DC, read-only routing for reports, In-Memory OLTP for hot paths.
**Visual:**
```
Bank SQL Server architecture (AG + sync/async + reporting):

  DC1 (primary data center):
    +---- Primary (RW) ----+   +---- Sync Sec (RO) ----+
    | In-Memory OLTP for   |   | Columnstore idx for   |
    | trading core (orders,|   | reporting queries     |
    | positions)           |   |                       |
    | sync-commit -------->|   | acks every commit     |
    +----------------------+   +-----------------------+
              |                          |
              +--------- Listener -------+
                        (RW -> P, RO -> S1)

  DC2 (DR):
    +---- Async Sec (RO) ----+
    | lag ~1s (DR only)      |
    | async-commit           |
    +------------------------+

  Quorum: file-share witness in 3rd location (Azure)
  Failover: P dies -> S1 promoted in 5-30s, listener reroutes
  DR: DC1 lost -> manual failover to DC2 (accept ~1s data loss)

  Reporting:
    + real-time (dashboards): read-only routing to S1
    + heavy analytics (EOD): dedicated async replica + columnstore
    + no impact on trading primary

  Trading path: app -> listener -> P (sync write, zero loss)
  Reporting path: app -> listener -> S1 or dedicated replica
```

### Q2. A 5 TB SQL Server data warehouse is slow; aggregations take minutes. How do you speed it up?
**Answer:** Convert the largest fact tables to **clustered columnstore indexes** — this is the single biggest win for SQL Server analytical workloads. Steps: (1) **Identify hot fact tables** — `sys.dm_db_index_usage_stats` shows which tables are scanned most. Focus on the top 5-10 fact tables. (2) **Convert to clustered columnstore** — `CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX idx_cc ON fact_sales;` (drops the existing clustered index). The table is now stored column-by-column with compression and batch mode. Expected: 5-10x compression (5 TB -> 1 TB on disk) and 10-100x scan speed. (3) **Build nonclustered B-Tree indexes for point lookups** — if some queries do `WHERE order_id = 42` (point lookup), add a nonclustered B-Tree on `order_id`. Columnstore is bad for point lookups; B-Tree is good. (4) **Partition by date** — `PARTITION BY RANGE (sale_date)`; queries that filter by date touch only relevant partitions (partition elimination). Also enables fast partition switching for data loading (load into a staging table, switch in atomically). (5) **Update statistics** — columnstore statistics are different from B-Tree; ensure they're fresh. (6) **Tune batch mode** — verify queries use batch mode (not row mode) via `EXPLAIN`; certain operators force row mode. (7) **Add memory** — columnstore batch mode is memory-intensive; the server may need more RAM. (8) **Consider Aggregations** (Analysis Services / Power BI) for repeated dashboard queries — pre-aggregate at load time. (9) **For HTAP** (mix OLTP + OLAP) — use nonclustered columnstore on a rowstore table; the OLTP path uses B-Tree, the OLAP path uses columnstore. Real-world: this transformation is standard for SQL Server data warehouses; Microsoft docs recommend columnstore for any fact table >1M rows.
**Visual:**
```
SQL Server DW optimization (5TB slow -> fast):

  Before (rowstore B-Tree):
    Fact tables (sales, events, clicks) as B-Tree
    Aggregations (SUM, GROUP BY) -> minutes (full table scans)
    5TB on disk

  After (clustered columnstore):
    1. CREATE CLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE INDEX ON fact_sales;
       -> 5-10x compression (5TB -> 1TB)
       -> 10-100x scan speed (batch mode, column pruning)
    2. Add nonclustered B-Tree for point lookups (order_id)
    3. Partition by date (PARTITION BY RANGE sale_date)
       -> partition elimination for date-filtered queries
       -> atomic partition switch for data loading
    4. Update columnstore statistics
    5. Verify batch mode in execution plans
    6. Add RAM (columnstore is memory-intensive)

  Result: aggregations from minutes to seconds
          disk usage from 5TB to 1TB

  For HTAP (mixed OLTP+OLAP):
    - keep rowstore for OLTP
    - add NONCLUSTERED COLUMNSTORE for OLAP scans
    - SQL Server uses the right one per query

  Microsoft recommendation: columnstore for any fact table >1M rows
```

### Q3. You're migrating from on-prem SQL Server to Azure SQL Database. What changes?
**Answer:** Azure SQL Database is fully-managed SQL Server (PaaS): Microsoft handles patching, backups, HA, scaling. Migration steps: (1) **Assess compatibility** — run Data Migration Assistant (DMA); it flags T-SQL features not supported in Azure SQL DB (e.g., SQL Agent jobs, cross-database queries, some system stored procs). Azure SQL Managed Instance (MI) supports more features than Azure SQL DB for lift-and-shift. (2) **Choose the right target** — Azure SQL DB (single database, simplest) for new apps; Azure SQL MI (instance-scoped, near-100% on-prem compat) for lift-and-shift; SQL Server on Azure VM (IaaS) for full control. (3) **Migrate schema + data** — Database Migration Service (DMS) does online migration (CDC from on-prem to Azure, cutover when caught up). (4) **Connection string change** — replace on-prem server name with Azure server (`mydb.database.windows.net`); add `Encrypt=True` and `TrustServerCertificate=False` (Azure requires TLS). (5) **Authentication** — Azure Active Directory auth (recommended for cloud) replaces Windows auth; SQL logins still work. (6) **HA is automatic** — Azure SQL DB has built-in HA (replica within region, automatic failover); no need to set up AGs. (7) **Backups are automatic** — point-in-time restore to any second in the last 7-35 days; no need for manual backup jobs. (8) **Performance tiers** — choose DTU or vCore model; vCore is recommended (right-size compute + storage independently). (9) **Tuning** — enable Query Store (tracks query performance over time); use Automatic Tuning (Azure creates/drops indexes automatically based on usage). (10) **Cost** — pay-per-hour; can be cheaper than on-prem for variable workloads (scale up during peak, down at night). Trade-offs: less control (no OS access, limited server-level config), some T-SQL features unavailable, network latency from app to Azure (must be in same region). Real-world: most enterprises migrate to Azure SQL MI for compat; new apps use Azure SQL DB.
**Visual:**
```
On-prem SQL Server -> Azure SQL Database migration:

  Assessment:
    - Data Migration Assistant (DMA) flags incompatible features
    - choose target: SQL DB (new app), SQL MI (lift-shift), VM (IaaS)

  Migration:
    - Database Migration Service (DMS) does online migration
    - CDC from on-prem to Azure, cutover when caught up
    - schema + data + log stream

  Changes:
    + connection string: mydb.database.windows.net (was on-prem)
    + auth: Azure AD (replaces Windows auth) or SQL logins
    + TLS required (Encrypt=True)
    + HA: built-in (no AG setup needed)
    + backups: automatic (PITR 7-35 days)
    + performance: vCore model (compute + storage independent)
    + tuning: Query Store + Automatic Tuning

  Trade-offs:
    - less control (no OS access, some server config unavailable)
    - some T-SQL features unavailable (SQL Agent, cross-DB queries
      in SQL DB; available in SQL MI)
    - network latency (must keep app in same Azure region)
    - cost: pay-per-hour (can be cheaper for variable workloads)

  Real-world:
    + new apps: Azure SQL DB (simplest, fully managed)
    + lift-and-shift: Azure SQL MI (near-100% compat)
    + full control: SQL Server on Azure VM (IaaS)
```

### Q4. A retail company's SQL Server primary is saturated during Black Friday. Reads are 95 % of load. How do you scale?
**Answer:** Reads at 95 % means read replicas are the answer, not vertical scaling of the primary. Architecture: (1) **Add AG secondaries** — already-running AG can have up to 8 secondaries; add 3-5 more to handle the read load. (2) **Read-only routing** — the AG listener routes read-only connections to secondaries; the app marks read-only transactions explicitly (`ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly` in connection string) so the listener routes correctly. (3) **Read Scale-Out** — even without AG, SQL Server 2016+ has "Read Scale-Out" availability groups (no WSFC required, just for read scaling, no HA failover). (4) **Caching layer** — for hot reads (product catalog, prices), add Redis/Elasticache; cache for 1-5 minutes. Most read load evaporates. (5) **Cross-region replicas** — for global users, add cross-region async secondaries (lower latency for EU/Asia users). (6) **Columnstore for analytics** — if some "reads" are analytical (sales reports), move them to a columnstore-indexed replica; 10-100x faster, no impact on primary. (7) **Vertical scaling as last resort** — bump up the primary's instance size (more cores, RAM); costly but immediate. (8) **Connection pooling** — ensure the app uses connection pooling ( SqlClient Pooling=true) to avoid connection churn on Black Friday spikes. (9) **Pre-warm** — before Black Friday, run a load test; identify hot queries and pre-build caches. (10) **Queue writes** — for non-critical writes (page views, click tracking), queue to Kafka and batch-insert later (decouples write spikes from primary load). Real-world: retailers like Amazon, Walmart prepare for Black Friday by scaling read replicas ahead of time and pre-warming caches; the primary handles only the ~5 % writes (orders, payments).
**Visual:**
```
Retail SQL Server scaling for Black Friday (95% reads):

  Before:
    1 Primary (RW) at 100% CPU
    p99 latency = 5s (slow, customers abandoning carts)
    -> primary saturated on reads

  After (layered scaling):
    1 Primary (RW) at 30% CPU (writes only, ~5% of load)
    + 5 AG Secondaries (RO) handling 95% read load
    + Redis cache (catalog, prices) - 80% of reads hit cache
    + Columnstore replica for analytics
    + Cross-region async replicas for global users

  Routing:
    App connection string: ApplicationIntent=ReadOnly
    -> AG listener routes RO -> secondary (load-balanced)
    App connection string: (default, RW)
    -> AG listener routes RW -> primary

  Layered approach (in order of ROI):
    1. Redis cache for hot reads (catalog, prices) - 80% offload
    2. Add 3-5 AG secondaries + read-only routing
    3. Columnstore for analytical reads
    4. Pre-warm caches before BF (load test, identify hot queries)
    5. Queue non-critical writes to Kafka (batch insert later)
    6. Vertical scale primary (more cores, RAM) as last resort

  Result: primary at 30% CPU, p99 = 50ms, no customer impact
```

### Q5. Your team is debating SQL Server vs PostgreSQL for a new healthcare app. The org is on .NET + Windows + Azure. How do you decide?
**Answer:** Given the strong Microsoft-stack commitment, **SQL Server is the default choice** — the integration advantage is too large to ignore. Reasons: (1) **Active Directory integration** — healthcare staff use Windows accounts; SQL Server with Windows auth gives seamless SSO (no separate DB credentials). PostgreSQL can use LDAP/GSSAPI but the integration isn't as polished. (2) **.NET ecosystem** — Entity Framework, Dapper, and ADO.NET are first-class for SQL Server; tooling (SSMS, SQL Server Profiler, Query Store) is mature. PostgreSQL works with .NET but isn't the primary target. (3) **Azure SQL Database** — managed SQL Server in Azure, integrates with Azure AD, Azure Monitor, Azure Backup. Lifts the operational burden. (4) **Power BI / Excel** — healthcare analysts use Power BI and Excel for reports; both connect to SQL Server natively with better performance than PostgreSQL. (5) **Compliance** — HIPAA, HITRUST; Microsoft signs BAAs and has compliance certifications; Azure SQL Database has built-in compliance features (Transparent Data Encryption, Always Encrypted, Row-Level Security). PostgreSQL has equivalents but you assemble them. (6) **Always On AGs** — multi-database atomic failover (useful when patient records and claims are separate DBs that must fail over together). (7) **Existing team expertise** — if the team knows SQL Server, the productivity advantage is significant. Choose PostgreSQL if: the team is committed to open-source; the app needs pgvector (AI features) or PostGIS (location); cost is a primary concern; or the app is being built cloud-native on Linux containers (Kubernetes) and you want to avoid Microsoft dependencies. Real-world: most healthcare apps on the Microsoft stack use SQL Server; Epic, Cerner, and major EHRs run on SQL Server or Oracle.
**Visual:**
```
Healthcare app: SQL Server vs PostgreSQL (.NET + Windows + Azure):

  SQL Server (recommended for this stack):
    + Active Directory integration (Windows auth SSO for staff)
    + .NET / EF / Dapper first-class support
    + Azure SQL Database (managed, Azure AD integrated)
    + Power BI / Excel native connectivity
    + HIPAA / HITRUST compliance (Microsoft signs BAAs)
    + Always On AGs (multi-DB atomic failover)
    + TDE, Always Encrypted, Row-Level Security (built-in)
    + team expertise (if already on Microsoft stack)

  PostgreSQL (if these matter more):
    + open-source (no vendor lock-in, no licensing cost)
    + pgvector for AI (RAG on patient records)
    + PostGIS for location (hospital finder, geo queries)
    + cloud-native / Linux / Kubernetes deployment
    + stricter ANSI SQL compliance
    + free for development and production

  Decision factors:
    + existing stack: Microsoft -> SQL Server, Linux/cloud-native -> PG
    + AI features (pgvector): PG (unless wait for SQL Server 9.0+ vector)
    + geo features (PostGIS): PG
    + cost: PG (free), SQL Server ($7k/core Enterprise)
    + team expertise: usually decisive

  For this org (.NET + Windows + Azure + healthcare):
    -> SQL Server (Azure SQL Database)
    -> Azure AD auth, Power BI, HIPAA BAA, AG HA
```

### Q6. A T-SQL stored procedure that ran in 100 ms now takes 30 seconds after a data load. Diagnose.
**Answer:** Sudden procedure slowdown after a data load suggests stale statistics, parameter sniffing regression, or a plan change. Diagnosis: (1) **Check Query Store** — SQL Server's Query Store tracks query performance over time; find the proc's recent executions and compare plan + duration to the baseline. Shows exactly when the regression started and which plan changed. (2) **Compare execution plans** — `EXEC sp_query_store_show_plans @proc_name`; if the plan changed (e.g., index scan became table scan), that's the cause. (3) **Update statistics** — `UPDATE STATISTICS your_table;` or `EXEC sp_updatestats;`. After a data load, statistics are stale; the planner uses old cardinality estimates and picks a bad plan. This is the most common cause. (4) **Parameter sniffing** — the proc was compiled with parameter X (selectivity 0.1%); now called with parameter Y (selectivity 50%); the cached plan for X is bad for Y. Fix: add `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` to recompile per call, or `OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN)` to use average selectivity, or use local variables to defeat sniffing. (5) **Check blocking** — `sp_who2` or `sys.dm_exec_requests` shows blocked sessions; a long-running transaction may be holding locks the proc needs. (6) **Check autostats** — if `AUTO_UPDATE_STATISTICS_ASYNC OFF` (default), stats update synchronously when stale, adding latency to the first query after a data load. (7) **Missing index** — `sys.dm_db_missing_index_details` suggests indexes; a new query pattern may need a new index. (8) **Memory pressure** — `sys.dm_os_memory_clerks` shows memory usage; if the buffer pool is full, the proc may be reading from disk. Fixes: (1) `UPDATE STATISTICS` (free, fixes 80 % of cases). (2) Add `OPTION (RECOMPILE)` to defeat parameter sniffing. (3) Add missing indexes. (4) Kill long-running blockers. (5) Clear proc cache: `DBCC FREEPROCCACHE` (last resort; affects all procs). Real-world: SQL Server's Query Store makes this diagnosis much easier than PostgreSQL's `pg_stat_statements`; it's a major advantage.
**Visual:**
```
T-SQL proc slowdown diagnosis (100ms -> 30s after data load):

  1. Query Store: compare plan before vs after
     - plan changed? (e.g., index seek -> table scan)
     - when did regression start? (correlate with data load)

  2. Statistics stale? -> UPDATE STATISTICS t; (most common cause)
     - data load changes cardinality, stats lag, plan regresses
     - autostats may not have triggered yet
     - fix: UPDATE STATISTICS or EXEC sp_updatestats

  3. Parameter sniffing?
     - proc compiled with param X (selective), now called with Y (broad)
     - cached plan bad for Y
     - fix: OPTION (RECOMPILE) per call
            OPTION (OPTIMIZE FOR UNKNOWN) - average selectivity
            local variables - defeat sniffing

  4. Blocking? sp_who2 / sys.dm_exec_requests
     - long-running txn holding locks?
     - fix: kill blocker, set isolation level

  5. Missing index? sys.dm_db_missing_index_details
     - new query pattern needs new index?

  6. Memory pressure? sys.dm_os_memory_clerks
     - buffer pool full, reading from disk?

  Fixes (priority):
    + UPDATE STATISTICS (free, 80% of cases)
    + OPTION (RECOMPILE) for parameter sniffing
    + add missing index
    + kill long-running blockers
    + DBCC FREEPROCCACHE (last resort, clears all cached plans)

  SQL Server advantage: Query Store makes this much easier
                       than PostgreSQL's pg_stat_statements
```

### Q7. Your enterprise has 500 SQL Server instances. How do you manage them at scale?
**Answer:** At 500 instances, manual management is impossible; you need centralized tooling. Architecture: (1) **SQL Server Central Management Server (CMS)** — register all instances in a CMS; run T-SQL across all of them from SSMS (e.g., check disk space on all 500). (2) **PowerShell + dbatools** — `dbatools` is a community PowerShell module for SQL Server management; script common operations (backup, restore, index rebuild, migration) across all instances. Idempotent and scriptable. (3) **SQL Server Management Studio (SSMS) policy-based management** — define policies (e.g., "all instances must have `MAXDOP = 4`") and check compliance across the fleet. (4) **Azure Arc for SQL Server** — register on-prem SQL Server instances with Azure Arc; manage them from Azure (Monitor, Defender, advanced security). Gives a single pane of glass for on-prem + Azure SQL. (5) **Monitoring** — SQL Sentry, Redgate SQL Monitor, or open-source (Prometheus + sql_exporter) for centralized metrics and alerting. (6) **Backup automation** — use Ola Hallengren's Maintenance Solution (community standard); scripts full/diff/log backups with verification. Centralize backup targets (Azure Blob, S3). (7) **Patching** — SQL Server Cumulative Updates quarterly; test in dev, roll out via WSFC rolling patches (one node at a time, no downtime for AGs). (8) **Cost management** — track per-instance cost (licensing, Azure consumption); consolidate underutilized instances. (9) **Standardization** — define a "gold configuration" (security settings, maxdop, cost threshold, model database defaults); apply to all new instances. (10) **Disaster recovery drills** — quarterly DR tests for the top 50 critical instances; verify backups restore, AGs fail over, RTO/RPO met. Real-world: large enterprises (banks, retailers) use a combination of dbatools + CMS + Azure Arc; the largest shops build custom automation on top. Trade-off: 500 instances is expensive (licensing + ops); consolidation (merge small instances into fewer larger ones) often reduces cost.
**Visual:**
```
Managing 500 SQL Server instances at scale:

  Centralization:
    + Central Management Server (CMS) - register all 500
    + Azure Arc - manage on-prem + Azure from one pane
    + PowerShell + dbatools - script ops across fleet
    + Policy-Based Management - enforce config compliance

  Monitoring (one pane):
    + SQL Sentry / Redgate / Prometheus+sql_exporter
    + centralized metrics: CPU, memory, disk, slow queries
    + alerting: lag, blocking, failed jobs, low disk

  Backup automation:
    + Ola Hallengren's Maintenance Solution (community standard)
    + full/diff/log backups with verification
    + centralized backup target (Azure Blob, S3)

  Patching (quarterly CU):
    + test in dev -> roll to prod
    + WSFC rolling patches (one node at a time, no downtime)

  Standardization:
    + "gold configuration" (maxdop, cost threshold, security)
    + apply to all new instances
    + policy-based compliance checks

  DR drills:
    + quarterly test for top 50 critical instances
    + verify backup restore, AG failover, RTO/RPO

  Cost management:
    + track per-instance cost (licensing, Azure)
    + consolidate underutilized instances (merge small into fewer larger)

  Tooling stack:
    dbatools + CMS + Azure Arc + SQL Sentry + Ola Hallengren
    + custom PowerShell/Python automation on top
```
